sections.overview: The shoebill is a wetland bird and the sole living member of Balaenicipitidae. Despite its stork-like silhouette, it is neither a stork nor a heron: evidence places it closer to pelicans. Its slate-grey body, long legs, and broad, shoe-shaped bill mark this marsh hunter.
sections.identification: Adults are about 1.2 m long and 1.1–1.4 m tall, with a wingspan near 2.4 m. BirdLife reports average mass of 5.6 kg for males and 4.9 kg for females. These reference figures are not universal maxima. Adults are mainly blue-grey, with darker flight feathers, a pale eye, and long, widely spread toes suited to walking over floating vegetation. The enormous bill has a deep, bulbous base, sharp cutting edges, and a hooked tip; males average slightly larger.
sections.habitat: It occupies freshwater swamps and seasonally flooded marshes across central and eastern Africa, from South Sudan south to Zambia. Dense reeds, sedges, or papyrus provide cover, while small open patches and floating plant mats offer places to fish and nest.
sections.diet: Fish dominate its diet, especially lungfish, bichirs, and catfish; it also takes water snakes and frogs, with other aquatic vertebrates reported less often. The bird waits motionless or walks slowly, then lunges down in a forceful forward collapse to seize prey in its bill.
sections.behavior: Usually solitary, shoebills keep space between feeding birds, even when a pair is nesting. A successful strike may bring up fish tangled with vegetation; the bird shakes plant matter free before swallowing. It is largely sedentary, though changing water levels can prompt local movements.
sections.reproduction: Pairs nest far apart, building broad platforms of wetland vegetation on floating mats or small mounds. Clutches hold one to three eggs, commonly two; both parents incubate and tend young. Often only one chick survives, as food shortage or sibling aggression limits the brood.
sections.ecology: The shoebill depends on a shifting mosaic: dense cover for concealment, fish-rich water, and open footing where it can recover after a lunge. In Bangweulu, Zambia, tracking found mostly short daily movements, linked to feeding and the search for suitable wetland patches.
sections.conservation: In its profile consulted in October2026, BirdLife International lists the shoebill as Vulnerable and reports an estimate of3,300–5,300 mature individuals. These are assessment estimates, not a new census. Wetland loss, hunting, nest disturbance, illegal capture and drought are identified pressures.
